blocks.x: Unlike transit networks in many global cities, New York City’s OMNY system currently tops out at a seven-day rolling fare cap. However, as the MTA looks to the future, officials are finally considering broader payment structures, including potential monthly or single-day fare caps.

Speaking at a Citizens Budget Commission (CBC) breakfast on September 22, MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber revealed the agency is working with its board to study new, “equity-oriented” fare approaches, marking a significant shift in the agency’s payment strategy.
Here’s what’s currently on the table, and what straphangers need to know about the system’s immediate future.
How the system works now

Currently, the MTA’s fare-capping system is straightforward but rigid: after paying for 12 rides—totaling $35 at the current base fare—using the exact same device or card, any subsequent bus or subway rides within a seven-day period are free.
For example: If your first ride is Monday morning, you’ll pay for your first 12 rides. Once you hit ride number 12, every bus or subway ride you take through Sunday is free.
Historically, Lieber defended this limitation.

He previously argued that the upfront cost of a traditional 30-day unlimited pass was fundamentally inequitable for lower-income New Yorkers who could not afford to pay over $100 all at once, noting that a rolling digital cap removes the risk of riders wasting money on pre-paid passes they don’t fully use.
What could change
With farebox revenue still trailing pre-pandemic levels and a scheduled transit fare hike looming in 2027, the MTA is searching for new ways to incentivize ridership.
At the CBC event, Lieber expressed a newfound willingness to leverage OMNY’s technology to offer a wider array of automatic discounts, according to Streetsblog.
Transit advocates have heavily pushed for this flexibility.

Lisa Daglian, Executive Director of the Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee to the MTA (PCAC), noted that riders frequently request a 30-day fare cap. Daglian also suggested expanding free transfer policies—such as allowing two free transfers on a multi-leg transit trip instead of just one.

Pointing to recent spikes in Long Island Rail Road ridership following expanded senior and family discounts, Daglian emphasized that “when you make it more affordable for people to ride, they’re going to ride,” as noted by Streetsblog.

MTA New York City Transit / Marc A. Hermann
MTA to launch OMNY education campaign
While future fare structures are studied, the MTA is actively addressing immediate frustrations with the current system.
According to amNY, Lieber acknowledged ongoing rider complaints and announced an upcoming public information campaign that will run on digital displays across the transit network.
The campaign will highlight the specific mechanisms riders must follow to unlock the current weekly cap:

Consistency is mandatory: Riders must use the exact same payment medium for every single tap. Switching between a physical credit card, Apple Pay, or an OMNY card will split your ride count and prevent the cap from triggering
Tracking your progress: Riders can create an account at OMNY.info to monitor their ride count and check their balances

Currently, turnstile screens do not display fare cap progress upon tapping. Lieber noted the MTA has faced software “struggles” with OMNY developer Cubic Transportation to bring real-time cap data to the turnstile screens.

Advocates remain frustrated by the delay, with amNY noting Daglian saying it’s well past time for Cubic to fix these lingering blind spots so riders have the information they need at the point of entry.
